title: A review of subjective evaluation, physiological indicators and cognitive performance in indoor light environment: The role of illuminance and correlated color temperature
review_question: To summarize the effects of indoor lighting conditions (illuminance and correlated color temperature) on subjective comfort, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance in indoor scenes (mainly schools and offices).
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Primary literature published from 2000 through December 2023; focused on effects of light exposure (illuminance and CCT) on subjective perception, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance; adhered to PICOS principles; experimental articles with at least one subjective evaluation, physiological indicator, or cognitive performance; experimental results with 95% confidence interval or sufficient data for calculation/verification. Excluded: duplicate entries, daylighting impact studies, research on daylighting control systems, studies of light factors other than illuminance and CCT, and studies not addressing illuminance or CCT.

synthesis_conclusions: Subjective comfort evaluations improve with higher illuminance, but visual comfort shows a 'diminishing returns' trend above 500lx. Subjective comfort also increases with higher CCT, with neutral CCT having an absolute advantage. High illuminance conditions can moderate positive mood and reduce subjective sleepiness and fatigue.

Higher illuminance and CCT lead to more active physiological manifestations, including increased melatonin suppression, elevated body temperature, elevated heart rate, and significant EEG changes. High illuminance and CCT should be avoided in nighttime lighting to minimize circadian disruption. Both can activate the brain and increase motivation, but also increase stress and stress reactions.

Cognitive performance generally improves with higher illuminance and CCT, though not for all cognitive tasks. Different tasks require different lighting conditions, but neutral CCT (3300K-5300K) is generally beneficial for cognitive performance improvement.

There is a correlation between subjective perception, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance. Comfortable lighting can enhance learning and performance. Light stimulation produces physiological responses that impact cognition and health, and physiological indicators can objectively verify comfort and performance.

The interaction between illuminance and CCT is significant, influencing visual comfort, cognitive performance, and physiological indicators (e.g., melatonin suppression). Optimizing this interaction can enhance cognitive performance and improve sleep quality.
evidence_gaps: Further study on the effects of long-term exposure to light on people, especially physiological parameters, in real-world settings (classrooms, offices).

Deeper exploration of the physiological mechanisms behind light's effects and the intrinsic connection between subjective, physiological, and cognitive evaluation indicators. Development of personalized lighting solutions based on physiological metrics like EEG signals.

Establishment of a unified evaluation standard (research methods, test content, results evaluation, statistical analysis) to enable direct comparison and more accurate quantitative conclusions across studies.
Comprehensive exploration of the co-action of multiple environmental factors (e.g., illuminance, CCT, sound, heat) and their interactions, rather than single-variable studies.
Expansion of research into extreme environments (e.g., extreme cold/heat, underground spaces) to understand light's effects in these contexts and inform design.

Multi-sensory interaction on indoor environmental perception

moderators.effect: Influences optimal lighting conditions and cognitive performance outcomes.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Different reading tasks require different optimal lighting conditions. WM load affects performance. Attention and memory tasks have different light requirements.

moderators.effect: Affects psychological variables, melatonin suppression, heart rate, and cognitive performance.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Bright light effects on psychological variables independent of time, but heart rate increased at night, not day. Morning light affects CBT and melatonin differently than afternoon light. Longer exposure time leads to greater melatonin inhibition.

moderators.effect: May influence the effect of bright light on sleepiness and alertness.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Electrocardiographic indices in the elderly do not change significantly under most light conditions. Pupil diameters are affected by age.

moderators.effect: The interplay between illuminance and CCT, and other IEQ factors (sound, heat) significantly influences outcomes.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Various lighting combinations can produce similar visual experiences. Interaction between illuminance and CCT affects visual comfort, cognitive performance, and physiological indicators.

limitations: Most existing studies are laboratory-based with limited exposure durations (<2h); long-term effects of artificial lighting in real settings (classrooms/offices) are understudied, especially on physiological parameters.
Existing articles primarily focus on changes in physiological indices due to lighting, with less involvement in the underlying physiological mechanisms.

While 70.5% of the reviewed literature studied two or more subjective feelings, physiological indicators, and cognitive performance, the interrelationship among these three aspects and their inner mechanisms were not deeply discussed.
